pharm: Iron salt (ferrous sulfate/fumarate/gluconate, carbonyl iron); essential mineral for hemoglobin synthesis
quick: Iron-deficiency anemia: ~100-200 mg elemental iron/day in divided doses (e.g., ferrous sulfate 325 mg = ~65 mg elemental, 1-3x/day)
Best on empty stomach for absorption; may take with food if GI upset
Commonly recommended; ~27-60 mg elemental iron/day for prophylaxis/treatment
No specific oral adjustment; in CKD oral iron often poorly effective (IV iron preferred)
No specific adjustment; avoid in iron-overload states
Alcohol may increase iron absorption; avoid excess
Hemoglobin, ferritin, transferrin saturation; reticulocyte response at ~1-2 weeks
summary: Oral elemental iron replaces body iron stores to treat and prevent iron-deficiency anemia. Dose is expressed as elemental iron; salts differ in elemental fraction (ferrous sulfate ~20%, fumarate ~33%, gluconate ~12%). Absorption is better on an empty stomach and with vitamin C; GI intolerance is the main limitation.
indications: Prevention of iron deficiency (pregnancy, blood loss, increased demand)

dosage.n: Continue 3-6 months after Hb normalizes to replete stores; alternate-day dosing may improve absorption/tolerability

admin: Take on an empty stomach (1 h before or 2 h after meals) when tolerated for best absorption
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) or citrus juice enhances absorption
Separate from antacids, calcium, tea/coffee, dairy, and certain antibiotics by ~2 h
Liquid forms: dilute and use a straw to limit tooth staining; rinse mouth after
moa: Iron is incorporated into hemoglobin, myoglobin and iron-containing enzymes. Supplemental ferrous iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, replenishing depleted iron stores and supporting erythropoiesis.

absolute: Hemolytic anemias not due to iron deficiency
monitor: Serum ferritin/transferrin saturation to avoid overload

preg: Iron deficiency is common in pregnancy and supplementation is widely recommended. Elemental iron ~27-60 mg/day is used for prophylaxis/treatment per antenatal guidance.
lact: Compatible with breastfeeding; supplemental doses are considered safe for the infant.
renal: No adjustment for oral iron in normal renal handling; in CKD oral iron is often poorly effective and IV iron is frequently preferred.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment; avoid in iron-overload-associated liver disease.

moderate: Levothyroxine, bisphosphonates, methyldopa, levodopa, penicillamine (reduced absorption of either drug)
minor: Tea, coffee, eggs, dairy reduce absorption
interactions.food: Empty stomach optimal; vitamin C enhances, phytates/polyphenols/calcium inhibit absorption
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may increase iron absorption; avoid excess
interactions.diagnostics: Darkens stools (may affect occult blood test interpretation); affects serum iron studies during therapy

emergency: Acute iron overdose (especially in children) - GI corrosion, shock, hepatotoxicity, metabolic acidosis

monitoring: Hemoglobin and reticulocyte count (response by 1-2 weeks)
counsel: Take on an empty stomach if tolerated; pair with vitamin C/orange juice
Expect darker stools - this is harmless
Separate from antacids, calcium, dairy, tea, and certain antibiotics
KEEP OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN - accidental overdose can be fatal
pk: Reticulocyte rise in ~3-10 days; Hb improvement over weeks
Serum iron peaks ~2-4 h after a dose
Iron is recycled; no fixed elimination half-life (minimal daily losses)
Stores repleted over 3-6 months of therapy
Room temperature; keep tightly closed and away from children
pearls: Always confirm whether a dose is elemental iron vs salt: ferrous sulfate 325 mg = ~65 mg elemental, fumarate 325 mg = ~106 mg, gluconate 325 mg = ~36 mg.
Alternate-day, once-daily dosing may improve fractional absorption and reduce GI side effects (hepcidin effect).
No reticulocyte response by ~2 weeks suggests non-adherence, malabsorption, ongoing blood loss, or wrong diagnosis.
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered; if near the next dose, skip it - do not double up.
overdose: Acute iron overdose is a medical emergency, especially in children. Stages: GI corrosion (vomiting, bloody diarrhea), apparent recovery, shock/metabolic acidosis/hepatic failure, then late GI scarring. Manage with supportive care and IV deferoxamine chelation for significant ingestion; contact poison control.
